slides.title: So, what is an AI agent?
slides.definition: A system that uses a language model to decide its own next steps, and takes actions with tools, until it reaches a goal.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A new colleague on the support team: you give them a goal and access to the order system, and they work out the clicks themselves.

slides.narration: Here is the definition we will use for the whole course. An AI agent is built around a large language model, or LLM: a model that reads and writes text. The model decides the next step itself, instead of following a script that someone wrote in advance. It takes actions through tools, such as looking up an order or searching a policy document. And it keeps going until it reaches a goal, like answering Ana with her real order status. Think of a new colleague on the support team. slides.title: The agent loop

note.text: Round again until the goal is met, or until a limit you set says stop.

slides.narration: Under the hood, every agent runs the same simple loop. First, it perceives: it reads what is in front of it, like Ana's message. Then it decides: given the goal, what is the most useful next step? Then it acts: it calls a tool, such as the order lookup, or it writes the reply. The result of that action is new information, so the loop starts again. Scout perceives the order details, decides it now knows enough, and acts by replying. The loop ends when the goal is met, or when a limit you set tells it to stop.

slides.title: How much should an agent do alone?
slides.lead: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. You choose where to set it.

bullets.text: Read only: look up orders and tracking, change nothing
Draft: write a reply that a person checks and sends
Act with approval: refunds over $200 wait for a person
Act alone: only small steps that are easy to undo

aside.label: Rule of thumb
aside.text: Give an agent the least power that does the job, and widen it as you learn to trust it.

slides.narration: Autonomy means how much an agent may do on its own, and it is a dial, not a switch. At the low end, an agent only reads: it looks up orders and tracking, and changes nothing. One step up, it drafts a reply, and a person checks it before it is sent. Higher still, it takes real actions, but risky ones wait for approval, like Orbit's refunds over two hundred dollars. Acting completely alone only makes sense for small steps that are easy to undo, because models can be wrong. A good rule: give an agent the least power that does the job, and widen it as you learn to trust it.

notes: A chatbot replies with text, a workflow follows steps a person wrote in advance, and an agent decides its own steps as it goes.

slides.title: What agents do well, and where they struggle

left.label: Good at
points: Working at any hour, at scale

slides.narration: Before we pick a first job, let's be honest about strengths and weaknesses. Agents are good at understanding messy requests written in plain language. They are good at choosing which lookup to make next, and at drafting replies and summaries. And they work at any hour, on hundreds of requests at once. But they struggle with facts they have no way to look up, and they can fill the gap with a confident guess. Long tasks with many steps give more chances for one step to go wrong. And judgement calls with real money or safety at stake still belong with people.

slides.title: Three signs of a good first agent job
slides.lead: Before you build anything, check the job against three questions.

bullets.text: Repetitive: it comes up many times a week, each time a bit different
Needs lookups: the answer lives in a system, not in the question
Recoverable: a mistake is easy to spot and cheap to fix

aside.label: If it fails the test
aside.text: A person, a help page or a simple workflow probably does the job better.

slides.narration: So how do you choose a good first job for an agent? First, it is repetitive: it comes up many times a week, and each time it is a little different. Second, it needs lookups: the answer lives in a system, like an orders database, not in the question itself. Third, mistakes are recoverable: if the agent gets one wrong, someone can spot it and fix it cheaply. A job that fails these checks is usually better done by a person, a help page or a simple workflow.

note.text: Then it runs again with the longer text. A 300-word reply is about 400 of these steps.

slides.narration: A large language model, or LLM, has one core job: given some text, predict what comes next. It starts with your text, such as a customer asking where her order is. That text is cut into small pieces called tokens. The model reads all the tokens and gives every possible next token a score for how likely it is. One token is chosen and added to the end of the text. Then the whole thing runs again with the slightly longer text, until the reply is complete. A three hundred word reply takes about four hundred of these steps.

slides.title: What is a token?

parts.text: About three quarters of a word

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: Lego bricks: the model has a fixed box of pieces, and every reply is snapped together one brick at a time.

slides.narration: You will hear the word token constantly when you build with models, so let us pin it down. Common words, like order or boots, are usually a single token. note.text: Picking among likely tokens is called sampling. It is why wording varies from run to run.

slides.narration: Let us slow the loop down and watch one turn of it. First, the model reads everything so far: your prompt, plus any part of the reply it has already written. Next, it scores every token it knows, perhaps ninety percent for one word and tiny chances for thousands of others. Then one token is picked, usually a very likely one, but not always the single top choice. That token is added to the text, and the loop goes round again. It stops when the model writes a special end token, or when it reaches the length limit you set. slides.narration: Choosing a model means weighing three things, separately for each step your agent takes. First, quality: can this model do this step well, every time? A customer in live chat notices a slow reply, while an overnight report does not care. Third, cost: the price per token, times the tokens per call, times the calls per day. One ticket costs a fraction of a cent, but thousands a day add up.

note.text: Switch a step only when your tests show the cheaper model still gets it right.

slides.narration: So which model should Scout use? Here is a rule of thumb that works well. A cheap wrong answer is not a saving.

slides.narration: Prompt engineering sounds technical, but it is mostly clear writing for a very literal reader. First, be specific: say exactly what you want, not roughly what you mean. Second, give context: the facts it needs, who the reader is, and why the task matters. Third, show examples, because one or two good answers teach style faster than a paragraph of rules. Fourth, name the output format: how long, what layout, and which fields. Fifth, break big tasks into smaller steps the model can take one at a time. A good test is to imagine handing your prompt to a smart new colleague on their first day: would they know what to do?

slides.title: What is a JSON schema?
slides.definition: A description of the exact shape an answer must have: its fields, their types, and which ones are required.

slides.narration: How do you score the chunks? There are two common ways. The simple way is keyword scoring: count the words each chunk shares with the question. The real-project way is embeddings: a model turns each chunk into a list of numbers that captures its meaning. Chunks with similar meaning get similar numbers, so a question finds them even in different words. Those numbers live in a vector store, such as Chroma or pgvector, which searches millions of chunks quickly.

slides.title: Reason and act
slides.definition: Reason and act: the agent thinks about the next step, takes one action, observes the result, and repeats.

analogy.text: A cook tasting as they go: season, taste, adjust, taste again, and stop when it's right.

slides.narration: There is no single fix for prompt injection, so you defend in three ways. First, keep rules and data apart: the rules live in the system prompt, and that prompt says customer text is only data. If refunds over two hundred dollars always need a person, a fooled model still cannot pay one out.

slides.narration: Latency is the time the customer waits, and in an agent it adds up across the steps. midQuiz.q: Which sign suggests Scout should be split into specialist agents?
options: After ten wholesale tools were added, Scout mixes up retail and trade prices
Scout takes three steps to answer a tracking question
Scout's daily cost doubled because ticket volume doubled
midQuiz.explain: Mixing up two jobs after the prompt and tool list grew is the classic sign of a crowded agent. Three steps is normal, and cost that tracks volume is expected.
midQuiz.hint: Look for the option where one agent is doing two different jobs badly.

midQuiz.q: What does the coordinator do in a multi-agent setup?
options: Runs every tool itself, then asks the specialists to check
Reads each request and passes it to the right specialist
Stores the full conversation history for all the agents
midQuiz.explain: The coordinator routes. It can be as simple as a classifier that reads the intent and passes a short summary to the right specialist.
midQuiz.hint: Think of a receptionist, not a manager who does everyone's work.

endQuiz.q: What is the main cost of moving from one agent to several?
options: Each agent needs its own separate API key
The agents can no longer use tools
Extra model calls, and more places to break and debug
endQuiz.explain: Routing and hand-overs add model calls, and a problem can now hide in any agent or between them. That is why you split only when one agent clearly struggles.
endQuiz.hint: What happens to the number of model calls, and to the trace, when work is passed between agents?

endQuiz.q: Why did this course have you write the tool loop by hand before using a framework?
options: Because frameworks cannot use custom tools
So you understand what a framework does inside, and can debug it
Frameworks are too slow for real agents
endQuiz.explain: Frameworks run the same loop, memory and guardrails you built. Knowing them from the inside means a framework saves you time instead of hiding problems.
endQuiz.hint: Think about the moment a framework does something you did not expect.

slides.title: The loop at the heart of Scout

center.label: Scout
center.sub: an agent, not just a chatbot

note.text: This is the ReAct loop from Module 4. Every agent framework runs some version of it.

slides.narration: Everything you built turns around one loop. Scout reads the customer's question, together with what it remembers from the conversation. It plans: it works out what it needs to know, and which tool could tell it. It acts by calling a tool, such as get order or track parcel. It observes the result, including any error, and decides whether it knows enough yet. Finally it answers within the policy and its limits, or hands over to a person. That is the react loop from Module 4, and every agent framework runs some version of it.

slides.title: What to learn next

note.text: The ideas carry over to any provider: OpenAI, Google or open models.

slides.narration: Where next? Here are four directions that build directly on Scout. Evaluations at scale: grow your ten test cases into hundreds, and use a model as a grader for answers that have no single right wording. Retrieval with embeddings: instead of matching words, search Orbit's documents by meaning, with a vector store such as Chroma or pgvector. More tools through MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for plugging an agent into ready-made tool servers, such as a help desk or a calendar. And multi-agent systems, for the day one agent is no longer enough. Everything you learned carries over to other providers, such as OpenAI, Google or open models; only the SDK calls change. Pick the direction that solves your next real problem, not the most exciting one.

slides.lead: The habits matter more than any one tool or framework.

bullets.text: Scope the agent to one job, and draw it before you code
Write test cases early, and re-run them after every change
Limits, approvals and logs on anything that runs unattended
Keep a person in the loop for what matters

aside.label: And remember
aside.text: Some jobs don't need an agent. A fixed workflow is simpler and cheaper when the steps never change.

slides.narration: Before the tools, a few habits that will serve you on every agent you build. Scope the agent to one clear job, and draw its parts before you write any code. Write test cases early, and re-run them after every change to the prompt, the tools or the model. Never leave an agent running unattended without step limits, spend limits, approvals and logs. Keep a person in the loop for decisions that matter, and make it easy for customers to reach one. And remember Module 1: some jobs do not need an agent at all, and a fixed workflow is simpler and cheaper.

midQuiz.q: In Scout's loop, what happens right after it calls a tool?
options: It observes the result, including any error, and decides what to do next
It starts a fresh conversation with the customer
It answers the customer straight away, whatever the tool said
midQuiz.explain: Read, plan, act, observe: after acting, Scout reads the result or the error and decides whether to call another tool, answer or hand off.
midQuiz.hint: Think of the four words in the loop, in order.

midQuiz.q: Owen asks for a $310 refund. Which part of Scout stops the money moving straight away?
options: The search_policy tool
The approval guard in your code
The system prompt on its own
midQuiz.explain: needs_approval() checks every refund call before it runs and holds anything over $200 for a person. The prompt asks for it; the code guarantees it.
midQuiz.hint: Which of these still works if the model gets confused?

endQuiz.q: Scout's word-matching search misses policy answers when customers use different words. Which next topic fixes that?
options: Retrieval with embeddings
Streaming replies
Multi-agent systems
endQuiz.explain: Embeddings let you search by meaning, so "send it back" can find the returns section even though the words differ.
endQuiz.hint: Which topic is about finding text by meaning rather than by matching words?

endQuiz.q: Orbit's help desk tool offers an MCP server. What does MCP give Scout?
options: A standard way to plug in ready-made tools
A way to run without an API key
A cheaper model for simple steps
endQuiz.explain: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting agents to tool servers, so Scout could use the help desk's tools without you writing each one.
endQuiz.hint: MCP is about tools, not models or keys.
